title: Student Privacy & Campus Surveillance Privacy Hardening Checklist
metaDescription: Comprehensive checklist to protect student privacy from campus surveillance, proctoring software, and educational data collection.
intro: Modern education involves extensive digital monitoring through proctoring software, campus networks, and educational technology platforms. This checklist helps students protect their privacy while navigating school-issued devices, online exams, and campus surveillance systems.

items.task: Review school device monitoring policies
items.why: Schools often monitor everything on issued devices including browsing, keystrokes, and personal files. Understanding the extent helps you protect sensitive information.
items.howTo: Request a copy of your school's device monitoring policy. Look for sections on web filtering, keystroke logging, and file access. Ask IT staff about specific monitoring software installed.

items.task: Create separate user accounts for personal use
items.why: Mixing personal and academic activities on school devices creates privacy risks as schools can access all data on their systems.
items.howTo: If allowed, create a separate local user account for personal activities. Keep academic work in the school-managed account and personal browsing in your account.

items.task: Use portable privacy browsers for personal browsing
items.why: School-installed browsers often have monitoring extensions and content filters that track your online activities.
items.howTo: Download portable versions of privacy-focused browsers like Incognito Browser or Firefox to a USB drive. These run without installation and leave minimal traces on the device.

items.task: Disable or limit cloud sync for personal accounts
items.why: Personal cloud accounts syncing to school devices can expose your private files and data to school monitoring systems.
items.howTo: Log out of personal Google, Apple, or Microsoft accounts on school devices. If you must use them, disable sync for photos, documents, and browsing history.

items.task: Use encrypted external storage for sensitive files
items.why: Files stored on school devices can be accessed by administrators, and personal documents may violate acceptable use policies.
items.howTo: Use encrypted USB drives or external hard drives for personal files. Tools like VeraCrypt can create encrypted containers for sensitive documents.

items.task: Regularly clear browsing data and temporary files
items.why: Even with monitoring, regularly clearing data reduces the digital footprint of your personal activities on school devices.
items.howTo: Use built-in browser cleaning tools or third-party cleaners like CCleaner to remove browsing history, cache, and temporary files weekly.

items.task: Understand your proctoring software's data collection
items.why: Proctoring software like Respondus or Proctorio can access far more than just exam activity, including system information and biometric data.
items.howTo: Read the privacy policy of your proctoring software. Look for data collection scope, retention periods, and third-party sharing. Request specific details from your school if unclear.

items.task: Secure your testing environment
items.why: Proctoring software records your screen, camera, and microphone, potentially capturing sensitive information in your room or on your screen.
items.howTo: Remove personal documents from view, cover sensitive information on walls or desks, and close all unnecessary applications before starting the exam.

items.task: Use a dedicated device or clean user profile for exams
items.why: Proctoring software may access browser history, installed applications, and system information from your primary user account.
items.howTo: If possible, use a separate device for proctored exams. Otherwise, create a clean user profile with minimal personal data and applications installed.

items.task: Limit network access during proctored sessions
items.why: Some proctoring software monitors network traffic and may flag legitimate activities as suspicious, while also potentially accessing local network devices.
items.howTo: Disconnect other devices from your network during exams. Use a guest network if available, or consider using mobile hotspot to isolate the testing device.

items.task: Document any privacy violations or technical issues
items.why: Proctoring software can malfunction or overreach, and having documentation helps protect your academic standing and privacy rights.
items.howTo: Keep records of any unusual behavior, excessive permissions requested, or technical problems. Screenshot error messages and note dates and times of issues.

items.task: Request data deletion after exam completion
items.why: Many schools and proctoring companies retain exam recordings and biometric data longer than necessary for academic purposes.
items.howTo: Submit written requests to both your school and the proctoring company to delete your exam recordings and biometric data after grades are finalized.

items.task: Audit permissions for educational apps and platforms
items.why: Educational technology platforms often request excessive permissions and may share student data with third parties for non-educational purposes.
items.howTo: Review app permissions on your devices for educational platforms. Disable unnecessary permissions like location access, contact list access, or camera access when not needed for coursework.

items.task: Understand FERPA rights and limitations
items.why: FERPA provides some protection for student educational records, but has exceptions that allow data sharing without consent in many situations.
items.howTo: Read your school's FERPA notice and understand what constitutes educational records versus other data. Know that FERPA doesn't cover all student data collected by schools.

items.task: Minimize personal information in educational profiles
items.why: Educational platforms often allow optional personal information that increases privacy risks without improving educational outcomes.
items.howTo: Review your profiles on learning management systems and educational apps. Remove optional personal information like personal interests, photos, or contact information not required for coursework.

items.task: Use privacy-focused communication tools when possible
items.why: Many educational communication platforms retain message history and may analyze communications for various purposes beyond education.
items.howTo: For group projects or study groups, consider using privacy-focused alternatives like Signal for sensitive discussions. Keep required platform use to academic content only.

items.task: Regularly review and clean up digital assignments
items.why: Old assignments and projects stored on educational platforms may contain personal information or demonstrate evolving political or personal views.
items.howTo: Periodically review old submissions and remove any that contain sensitive personal information. Download important work for personal archives before deletion.

items.task: Monitor third-party integrations and data sharing
items.why: Educational platforms often integrate with third-party services, creating additional data sharing relationships that expand privacy risks.
items.howTo: Check your educational platform settings for connected third-party apps and services. Disconnect any that aren't essential for your current coursework.

items.task: Use VPN on campus networks
items.why: Campus networks often monitor, filter, and log all internet traffic, creating detailed profiles of student online activities.
items.howTo: Install a reputable VPN service on your devices before connecting to campus WiFi. Choose VPN providers with no-logging policies and strong encryption.

items.task: Understand campus surveillance systems
items.why: Modern campuses use extensive camera surveillance, WiFi tracking, and access card monitoring that can create detailed records of student movements and associations.
items.howTo: Request information about campus surveillance policies from student services. Learn about camera locations, data retention periods, and access procedures for your own records.

items.task: Manage WiFi and Bluetooth tracking
items.why: Campus systems can track device location through WiFi and Bluetooth signals, even when you're not actively connected to networks.
items.howTo: Turn off WiFi and Bluetooth when not needed. Use randomized MAC addresses if your device supports it. Consider airplane mode in sensitive locations.

items.task: Protect ID card and access data
items.why: Student ID cards often contain RFID chips that can be read without your knowledge, and access logs create detailed movement patterns.
items.howTo: Use RFID-blocking wallets or sleeves for your student ID. Be aware that card access creates logs, and consider cash transactions when privacy is important.

items.task: Be cautious with campus social media and check-ins
items.why: Social media posts, location check-ins, and campus app usage can create additional data points that supplement official surveillance systems.
items.howTo: Disable location services for social media apps on campus. Avoid checking in to sensitive locations, and review privacy settings for any campus-specific social platforms.

pro_tips: Keep personal and academic digital lives separate - use different browsers, accounts, and devices when possible to minimize data correlation.
Document everything - save copies of privacy policies, monitoring notices, and any privacy violations you experience for potential future complaints or legal action.
Know your rights under FERPA, but understand its limitations - it doesn't cover all student data and has many exceptions for data sharing without consent.
Build relationships with privacy-conscious classmates to share information about new monitoring systems and effective privacy strategies specific to your institution.
Consider the long-term implications of educational data collection - information collected now may affect you years later in employment, insurance, or other contexts.
